Novo Nordisk's Split Earnings Signal Leaves Investors Weighing a Buyback, a Guidance Lift and an Ins
sum: Novo Nordisk's third-quarter 2026 release landed with two profit figures pointing in opposite directions — and a share sale by its top scientist the same week gave shareholders one more data point to weigh. The stock fell 4.1% yesterday, though no specific trigger for that move has been established.

At the heart of the puzzle is the gap between the Danish drugmaker's adjusted and reported operating results. On a constant-currency basis, adjusted operating profit climbed 27%. Reported operating profit, measured the same way, fell 9%. Impairment charges of DKK 8.7 billion weighed on the reported line, according to Reuters.

Adjusted operating profit for the quarter came in at DKK 31,720 million. Revenue on the same basis totalled DKK 79,195 million, up 4% at constant exchange rates, with the Wegovy pill contributing DKK 5,394 million. The obesity franchise as a whole grew 22% — a pace that outstripped the group and offers a concrete marker for anyone betting the adjusted momentum can hold.

Guidance, too, hinges on which numbers you read. Novo Nordisk now expects both adjusted revenue and adjusted operating profit to land anywhere between 2% growth and a 2% decline in 2026, at constant currencies. The prior range ran from flat to a 6% drop. The lift moves the corridor in a friendlier direction, but a decline remains squarely inside it.

Adding to the mix, Executive Vice President and Chief Scientific Officer Martin Holst Lange sold 12,000 B-shares on Wednesday at DKK 285.00 apiece, according to media reports. The transaction pits a senior executive's selling against a company that just raised its outlook — a pairing that leaves the investment case resting less on the insider move itself than on whether the operating improvement carries through.

Capital returns tell a quieter story. Novo Nordisk has repurchased 41,714,179 B-shares for a cumulative DKK 11,564,364,801, part of a programme worth up to DKK 15 billion that began on 4 February 2026 and runs for twelve months. That ceiling is the planned envelope, not money already spent.

What comes next is a test of quality, not just quantity. Investors leaning optimistic will want the obesity business to keep expanding and that growth to flow through to earnings rather than revenue alone.

Novo Nordisk Buys Time: A 27% Profit Jump, a New CFO, and a Guidance Call Deferred to February
sum: Novo Nordisk delivered a third-quarter beat that sent its shares up 4.8% yesterday, but the more telling signal came from what management did not say. Chief executive Mike Doustdar declined to issue guidance for 2027, pushing that reckoning to the full-year results in February 2027. Between now and then, investors must decide whether the company's volume-led recovery can outrun the price cuts it has already scheduled for the U.S. market.

The headline numbers argue for optimism. Adjusted revenue for the third quarter of 2026 came in at DKK 79.2bn, a 4% increase at constant currencies. Adjusted operating profit grew far faster, climbing 27% at constant currencies to DKK 31.72bn — a margin performance that suggests the quarter was about more than top-line momentum. The Wegovy pill contributed DKK 5.39bn in revenue, and free cash flow exceeded DKK 28bn in the period.

Novo Nordisk also lifted its outlook for 2026, a move Reuters identified as a contributor to yesterday's share-price advance. The revised guidance now points to a range of -2% to +2% at constant currencies for both adjusted revenue and adjusted operating profit. That is a forecast which still permits contraction, a detail worth keeping in view before treating the quarter as the start of a durable upswing.

Not everyone read the beat as a buying opportunity. Jefferies reaffirmed its "Hold" rating and DKK 275 price target yesterday, while noting that consensus estimates could rise because the improved outlook sits above prior expectations. The distinction matters: higher earnings and revenue forecasts are one thing, an upgraded recommendation is another. The broker's measured response stands in contrast to the market's more enthusiastic reception.

The growth itself deserves closer scrutiny than the headline percentage suggests. Roughly 60,000 weekly prescriptions flowed through the Medicare Bridge programme, meaning a meaningful slice of the volume gain came from a single access channel rather than from broad-based demand. Medicare coverage for seniors began in mid-2026, and next year it could contribute to sales across a full twelve-month period for the first time — a tailwind, but also a concentration risk if the rest of the market stays soft.

Novo Nordisk's November Ledger: Revenue Guidance Holds the Gavel Before Science Makes Its Case
sum: Novo Nordisk investors face a split-screen test in the coming weeks, and the order in which the two halves resolve matters more than either one alone. On one side sits the commercial question — whether the Danish drugmaker's 2026 revenue guidance can carry near-term expectations. On the other sits the scientific one — whether a dense calendar of conference presentations can demonstrate a clinical profile strong enough to answer Eli Lilly's latest challenge.

The two are not interchangeable. Research momentum can underpin a longer-term view, but it cannot substitute for evidence that commercial forecasts are being met. That distinction frames everything between now and mid-November.

Novo Nordisk has scheduled nine-month 2026 results for 4 November, and the revenue outlook for the full year is the number that matters most. An upgrade would read very differently from an unchanged forecast or a cut — and none of those outcomes is settled yet. Just as telling would be the reasoning behind any revision, since only the explanation would reveal how much of the forward case rests on demand for existing products.

The link between Wegovy and the company's planned real-world studies deserves particular attention. Novo intends to present treatment experience with the Wegovy pill, data that could help position the product beyond the confines of controlled trials. What such findings cannot do is stand in for reported sales.

Hence a clear sequence for anyone weighing the shares: the business outlook has to hold up first. Only then does it make sense to ask whether additional research data meaningfully extends the story. Blur the two layers, and scientific progress risks being booked prematurely as commercial success.

The competitive backdrop sharpened on Thursday, when Eli Lilly reported that its retatrutide outperformed Ozempic in a head-to-head phase 3 study of adults with type 2 diabetes. According to Lilly, retatrutide delivered a greater reduction in A1C, while weight loss came in at more than double that achieved with Ozempic 2 mg.

That result speaks to one specific comparison, not a blanket verdict on Novo's entire pipeline. Still, it raises the bar: what counts now is which durable advantages Novo can demonstrate with data of its own.

OMER Stock Surges 5% After Hours On Novo Nordisk Deal Windfall And Drug Launch Optimism
sum: Shares of Omeros Corporation (OMER) rose 5% after hours on Tuesday after the company expressed optimism for its deal with Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk and regarding its other drugs.
The company reported net income for the fourth quarter of $86.5 million, compared to a net loss of $31.4 million in the corresponding quarter of 2024.

The company said that its fourth quarter results include a net gain of $237.6 million tied to the zaltenibart transaction with Novo Nordisk. Under the deal valued up to $2.1 billion, the Danish drugmaker received exclusive global rights in all indications to develop and commercialize Omeros’s zaltenibart and certain related antibodies and products.

The transaction was closed in November, triggering an upfront cash payment of $240 million. The company is now eligible to receive milestone payments and tiered royalties on annual global net sales of applicable products.

The company’s Yartemlea was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of hematopoietic stem cell transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy in adults and in children ages two years and older in December. Commercial distribution and sales of Yartemlea in the U.S. began in January. The drug is now being prescribed to both adult and pediatric patients across both hospital and outpatient settings, the company said, while adding that it has engaged several of its workforce to engage directly with transplant centers across the United States.
The company is now looking forward to an approval for the therapy from the European Medicine Agency by mid-2026.

“Following FDA approval of Yartemlea with a broad label and no boxed warning, REMS, or required vaccinations, our commercial launch is well underway, and patients who urgently need the drug are now able to access it,” said Omeros CEO Gregory A. Demopulos. “Our partnership with Novo Nordisk expands the breadth of indications being pursued for zaltenibart and has provided — and should continue to provide — substantial operating capital... These successes are expected to fuel the development of a growing portfolio of commercial products from our robust pipeline as we target positive cash flow in 2027.”

Novo Nordisk Clinches 2.7% Gain as J.P. Morgan Flags a Possible Upgrade and Buybacks Roll On
sum: Shares of Novo Nordisk advanced 2.7% to EUR 34.03 on Monday, a move that market participants struggled to pin to any single company-specific catalyst. The bounce offers little comfort against the broader trend: the Danish pharma group has shed 23% since the start of the year, leaving investors to debate whether the recent firmness marks the early stages of a bottom or merely a pause before further weakness.

Sentiment across the sector remains guarded, with traders split on whether current valuations represent an entry point or a warning sign of more downside ahead. Against that cautious mood, J.P. Morgan's Richard Vosser offered a counterweight. The analyst reiterated a Neutral rating and a DKK 275 price target, but held out the prospect that Novo Nordisk could deliver a strong third-quarter report and raise its full-year guidance — a scenario that would mark a sharp reversal from the skepticism that has dogged the stock for months.

Capital returns remain a visible source of support. Novo Nordisk disclosed Monday that it repurchased 1,225,000 of its own B shares between 28 September and 2 October. Under the wider program, the company reported holding 36,604,179 B shares acquired as of 2 October, at a cumulative cost of DKK 10,247,270,869. The buyback authority itself dates to 4 February 2026 and permits repurchases of up to DKK 15 billion over a twelve-month window.

Such measures demonstrate financial firepower, yet they cannot substitute for operational momentum. What matters more to the investment case is whether demand for the company's core diabetes and obesity medicines holds firm enough to shield operating margins from further pressure.

On the research front, Novo Nordisk has served up a string of promising data points. Roughly a week ago, it presented real-world findings on the oral formulation of semaglutide: patients who switched to the Wegovy pill recorded an average weight loss of 4.1% after three months. Separate results for the candidate CagriSema showed the compound reduced food cravings and fat tissue around internal abdominal organs, while early data suggested bone health remained stable despite substantial weight loss.

Novo Nordisk Stock Has Fallen Sharply, Does a Long-Term Opportunity Emerge?
sum: Novo Nordisk (NVO) once fell behind in the GLP-1 weight-loss drug competition, with its stock price down more than 70% from its peak and even below its level five years ago, leaving investors deeply worried. However, the company’s revenue and earnings per share have both achieved substantial growth over the past five years, and as the first company to launch a GLP-1 drug and an oral version, its research and development capabilities have already been proven. As the company adjusts its business model and lays out future new drugs, if long-term investors can withstand short-term volatility, the current deep pullback may constitute a rare opportunity rather than a value trap.

In the GLP-1 weight-loss drug field, Novo Nordisk is in a passive position. The company was the first to launch Wegovy, but failed to keep up with market demand, which gave generic drugs an opportunity to enter the U.S. market before patent protection expires. After competitor Eli Lilly launched a more effective GLP-1 drug, Novo Nordisk became an industry follower. Novo Nordisk gained a second chance with its oral GLP-1 drug, which reached the market earlier than Eli Lilly’s oral drug. However, the company announced that it would lower the price of its GLP-1 drugs and focus on sales volume. The weight-loss market may be extremely large, so sales volume matters and may ultimately offset the impact of price cuts. But in the short term, as the business model adjusts around GLP-1 drugs, Novo Nordisk’s financial performance may come under pressure, even though the oral version appears to be in strong demand.

Eli Lilly is using its success in GLP-1 to finance acquisitions, thereby broadening its business and now possessing a significantly deeper pipeline of potential candidate drugs. Novo Nordisk has acted less aggressively, with the most notable change being its name change to “Novo” to highlight a renewed focus on the company’s future. This move has not been particularly well received, and many may view it as little more than a superficial gesture. Recently, the company announced plans to launch multiple new drugs by 2030. If it can do so, the company will have new drugs on the market before its existing GLP-1 drugs begin to lose patent protection in the early 2030s.

Novo shares slide as drugmaker lays out post-Wegovy growth strategy
sum: Novo shares plummeted on Monday after the company's new long-term goals failed to ease investor concerns about its ability to compete in the increasingly crowded weight loss market it helped pioneer.

The Danish drugmaker said it aims to launch more than five drugs with "multi-blockbuster" potential by 2030 and generate more than 150 billion Danish kroner ($23 billion) in risk-adjusted pipeline sales by 2035, including current assets.
It also expects revenue growth between 2026 and 2030 to be in line with industry peers such as Eli Lilly, AstraZeneca, Amgen, Biogen, Merck, AbbVie, and Novartis.
Copenhagen-listed shares closed 7.7% lower on Monday, in their worst day since February.
"Investors hoped for a project 'miracle' that could turn the momentum around short term," Per Hansen, savings economist at Nordnet, told CNBC. "For obvious reasons that miracle does not exist."

CEO Mike Doustdar told investors at the company's Capital Markets Day in London that the "elephant in the room" was that semaglutide, the active ingredient in weight-loss and diabetes medicines Wegovy and Ozempic, will lose key patent exclusivity starting early next decade. The semaglutide patent expires in 2032 in the U.S., a market that accounted for more than half of Novo's overall sales last year.
This loss of exclusivity "is what's on most people's mind, and rightfully so," Doustdar said.

As Capital Markets Day Approaches, Can Novo Nordisk Stock Reverse Slump with New Strategy?
sum: Ahead of its London Capital Markets Day, Novo Nordisk faces mounting institutional pressure amid intensifying competition from Eli Lilly in the weight-loss market. With the stock down over 16% year-to-date and trading below key moving averages, investors demand clear strategies beyond recent workforce reductions. Analysts emphasize the necessity of accelerating new drug development, successful commercialization, and potential M&A to diversify revenues, as over 90% of sales rely on diabetes and obesity treatments. While management focuses on organizational restructuring and brand unification, the stock remains in a weak consolidation phase, with the $40.92 level acting as critical defensive support.
TradingKey - As Capital Markets Day approaches, Novo Nordisk (NVO) is facing increasingly evident pressure from institutional investors.

On September 21 local time, the Danish drugmaker will hold its Capital Markets Day in London to officially outline its new corporate strategy. This will also mark the first comprehensive presentation of the company's future direction to investors by newly appointed CEO Mike Doustdar.

Over the past few years, products like Ozempic and Wegovy propelled Novo Nordisk into a key player in the global weight-loss drug market, with its market capitalization once surpassing $600 billion. However, as Eli Lilly (LLY) continues to capture market share with Zepbound, Novo Nordisk's competitive edge in key markets like the United States has eroded, sending its stock price sharply lower. Today, investors are looking for management to present not just cost-cutting plans, but a product strategy capable of driving growth for years to come.

Eugen Uretzki, an investment analyst at Flossbach, believes that Novo Nordisk's most critical tasks are twofold: continuing to develop new drug assets, and demonstrating the ability to successfully commercialize them. He noted that against the backdrop of intensifying competition from Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk does not have much time left to wait for new products to mature organically.
This also explains why M&A has once again become a central focus for investors.

The brokerage moved the stock to Underweight from Equal-weight. It expects semaglutide to account for about 75% of Novo's sales in 2026, leaving the company exposed to the loss of exclusivity beginning in 2031.

Novo Nordisk Holds Its Capital Markets Day on September 21. Here’s What NVO Stock Needs to Show
sum: Now Live: Discover how much upside your favorite stocks could have using TIKR’s new Valuation Model (It’s free) >>>

Novo Nordisk (NVO) will put its whole strategy on the table in London on September 21, and it does so from a position almost no one expected a year ago: near the bottom of its 52-week range. The stock closed at $44.56 on September 9, closer to its $35.12 low than to the $64.16 high it touched twelve months back. What makes the setup strange is that the business underneath has started working again. Obesity sales grew 16% last quarter, the Wegovy pill is the strongest GLP-1 launch by volume the company has ever run, and management raised full-year guidance for the second time this year, though to a still-cautious 0% to -6% adjusted sales growth at constant currencies.

On September 7, Novo reported a successful pediatric obesity trial and, the same day, disclosed a second pipeline failure, and the shares slid over the sessions that followed, closing near $44.56 by September 9. Closing the gap between a franchise that is executing and a stock that will not respond is what Capital Markets Day has to do.

Novo delivered a clean beat in the second quarter, reported August 4. Revenue came in at DKK 78,488 million against a Street estimate of DKK 71,535 million, a 9.72% beat, and adjusted earnings per share of 6.18 topped the 4.98 consensus by 24%, per TIKR’s earnings data. Adjusted sales grew 7% at constant exchange rates and adjusted operating profit rose 11%.

Investors have been trained by a brutal 2026 to distrust good prints, and the reasons are on the record: a max drawdown of 44.84% on March 30, repeated pricing scares, and steady U.S. share loss to Eli Lilly. The quarter did not erase that memory. The oral launch is the clearest evidence it should start to. EVP of U.S. Operations Jamey Millar called the Wegovy pill “the strongest ever GLP-1 launch by volume,” now past five million total prescriptions with the latest million added in four weeks, and holding around 90% of the U.S. oral obesity market against an April competitor.

Novo Nordisk A/S Stock (NVO) Moved Down by 3.32% on Aug 26: Drivers Behind the Movement
sum: Novo Nordisk A/S (NVO) moved down by 3.32%. The Pharmaceuticals & Medical Research sector is down by 1.47%. The company underperformed the industry. Top 3 stocks by turnover in the sector: Eli Lilly and Co (LLY) down 3.52%; Moderna Inc (MRNA) down 6.92%; Merck & Co Inc (MRK) down 1.94%.

Novo Nordisk experienced downside pressure and elevated intraday volatility, reflecting ongoing market recalibration around its growth outlook and therapeutic leadership in the metabolic sector. The decline follows a broader repositioning by institutional investors who are weighing the company's solid long-term fundamentals against intensifying near-term operational headwinds. While the company continues to expand global distribution of its flagship obesity and diabetes franchises, persistent competitive pressures from rival therapies have heightened market sensitivity to gross-to-net realization and market share trends.

A primary driver behind the stock's weakness stems from margin compression and pricing dynamics in the pivotal U.S. healthcare market. Novo Nordisk faces sustained pricing pressure, increased rebate demands, and reduced insurance coverage for weight-loss medications, all of which have pressured gross margins relative to historical levels. Although management previously updated constant-currency expectations, full-year guidance continues to reflect a muted growth trajectory. Investors remain cautious as lower realized selling prices in North America offset volume gains from oral and injectable formulations, raising questions about top-line expansion through the remainder of the fiscal year.

Market sentiment has also been tempered by competitive developments and pipeline scrutiny. Key industry peers continue to aggressively capture market share with competing GLP-1 dual- and triple-agonist candidates, while agile clinical-stage biotechs advance alternative oral therapies. Recent pipeline adjustments and clinical data disclosures from next-generation programs have led analysts to re-examine Novo Nordisk's long-term competitive moat. Furthermore, following a short-lived rebound in previous sessions, intraday profit-taking combined with macroeconomic chatter regarding U.S. interest rate metrics further amplified selling pressure on high-profile healthcare ADRs.

sum: Novo Nordisk (NYSE:NVO), the Danish pharmaceutical giant behind Ozempic and Wegovy, edged nearly 2% higher during Friday's U.S. regular session after a federal judge threw out an antitrust lawsuit against Novo and Eli Lilly (NYSE:LLY). According to Reuters, the case was filed by Strive Specialties, which claimed the drugmakers unfairly limited access to compounded GLP-1 weight-loss drugs through exclusive telehealth partnerships.

The ruling removes one legal headache, but it is far from the final chapter. The judge dismissed Strive's complaint in its current form rather than ending the broader fight over compounded obesity drugs, leaving the door open for an amended complaint or an appeal. For investors, the lawsuit was never the main event anyway. The real battle is whether Novo can protect its blockbuster GLP-1 franchise as Lilly keeps turning up the competitive heat.

The valuation may be the bigger story. The accompanying GF Value chart estimates Novo's fair value at $110.54, while the stock changes hands around $46.86, putting it roughly 57.6% below that estimate. That discount suggests Wall Street has already baked plenty of pessimism into the shares after concerns over slowing obesity-drug momentum and pipeline execution. If management can deliver on its upgraded outlook and prove demand remains strong, today's beaten-down valuation could look overly harsh. Still, investors should think twice before treating the gap as a guaranteed bargain because even deeply discounted stocks can stay cheap if business fundamentals fail to improve.

The divide between Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk is widening after their latest earnings
sum: The diverging paths of two GLP-1 drugmakers were on full display this week.

Both Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk beat second-quarter estimates and raised their full-year outlooks. But while investors cheered Lilly's results, sending shares higher on Wednesday, they punished Novo a day earlier — underscoring a growing divide in Wall Street's confidence in the two obesity drug leaders.

As Lilly continues to exceed expectations and widen its edge in the obesity drug space, Novo is still racing to win back market share, restore investor confidence in its pipeline and chart a clear path toward long-term growth.
"While Novo raised guidance (as expected), the pipeline and path to sustainable growth remain less clear," BMO Capital Markets analyst Evan Seigerman said in a research note on Wednesday.

At stake is a global market that some analysts expect to be worth more than $100 billion by the 2030s. In the U.S., Lilly held a 60.9% share of the obesity and diabetes drug market in the second quarter, compared with Novo's 38.8%, according to Lilly's earnings presentation Wednesday.

Lilly reported another quarter of blistering growth, with resilient demand for its blockbuster diabetes treatment Mounjaro and obesity drug Zepbound pushing revenue up 48% from a year ago. The company also hiked its full-year revenue guidance, reinforcing investor confidence that its treatments can sustain their sales momentum despite lower prices in the U.S. — an issue that Novo is also facing.

"The print reinforces our view that Lilly remains best positioned to capture the majority of global incretin market growth," Bernstein analyst Courtney Breen said in a note on Wednesday, referring to the obesity and diabetes drug space.

Novo Nordisk tumbles as Wegovy sales miss, trial setback overshadow raised outlook
sum: Investing.com -- Novo Nordisk (CSE:NOVOb) (NYSE:NVO) hiked its full-year guidance, saying annual sales and operating profit should decline less than previously expected as demand for its weight-loss drugs continues unabated.

But shares fell 6% in U.S. trading Tuesday after the company's new Wegovy pill missed sales estimates and an experimental next-generation weight-loss drug delivered disappointing study results. The company's Copenhagen-listed shares fell 4.2% by 07:44 GMT after the market opened on Wednesday.

The Danish drugmaker now expects adjusted sales and operating profit to fall by up to 6% at constant exchange rates this year, an improvement from its prior forecast of a decline of 4% to 12% for both measures.

Sales of the oral version of Wegovy came in at 3.2 billion Danish kroner in the second quarter, equivalent to about $500 million, falling short of the 3.3 billion kroner analysts surveyed by FactSet had expected. The injectable form of Wegovy generated 19.48 billion kroner in sales during the quarter.
Novo also said its experimental drug CagriSema failed to match the blood-sugar-lowering effect of Eli Lilly's (NYSE:LLY) tirzepatide in a new study of people with Type 2 diabetes.

In the trial, CagriSema was noninferior to tirzepatide on the primary endpoint of weight loss, with patients losing 15.2% of their body weight versus 15.8% for tirzepatide. However, on the second primary endpoint — reduction in HbA1c, a measure of blood sugar control, CagriSema fell short, delivering a 1.9% reduction compared with 2.2% for tirzepatide.

"We expected CagriSema to show non-inferiority on both primary endpoints, but importantly, for Zepbound to numerically outperform on both co-primary endpoints. So, today's result came in less favorable for CagriSema than expected," Wolfe Research analyst Alexandria Hammond said in a note.

Novo Nordisk shares slide after guidance disappoints investors
sum: U.S.-traded shares of Novo Nordisk dropped about 6% on Tuesday after the Danish drugmaker released guidance that appeared to disappoint investors.

The company hiked its 2026 outlook, saying it expects adjusted sales to be down 6% to flat at constant exchange rates. Novo Nordisk previously said it anticipated adjusted sales would fall between 4% and 12%.
The drugmaker also said it expects adjusted operating profit to be in a range of down 6% to flat. It had previously anticipated that metric would drop between 4% and 12%, as well.

Notably, Novo also said it expects a sales decline in U.S. operations, citing current prescription trends for GLP-1 injections, "intensifying" competition and a negative impact from reduced obesity medicine coverage in Medicaid. The company also cited lower realized prices in the U.S., in part due to the landmark "most favored nation" drug pricing agreement it struck with President Donald Trump for its GLP-1s.

Novo Nordisk also announced key financial metrics for the second quarter and first half of 2026, ahead of an expected earnings release on Wednesday. Eli Lilly, its lead rival in the booming market for GLP-1 drugs, is also scheduled to post quarterly results on Wednesday.
The Danish drugmaker said second-quarter sales rose to 78.49 billion kroner ($12.09 billion), up 3% in constant currency. On an adjusted basis, sales climbed 7% during the period.

Novo said its newly launched pill version of its Wegovy weight loss drug raked in 3.22 billion kroner for the second quarter. That's slightly below the 3.27 billion kroner that analysts were expecting for the period, according to StreetAccount.

Novo Nordisk shares dive after heart medicine fails trial, dealing another blow to its pipeline
sum: Shares of Novo Nordisk fell as much as 10% on Friday after the drugmaker said a late-stage heart drug trial failed to reduce major adverse cardiovascular events, or MACE, compared to a placebo.

While the experimental medicine, ziltivekimab, did show some biological effect, it didn't translate into a statistically meaningful reduction in MACE, defined as cardiovascular death, non-fatal heart attack or non-fatal stroke, for patients with certain diseases, Novo said in a statement on Friday.
The missed endpoint is the latest blow to the Danish drugmaker, which is racing to restore investor confidence in its pipeline and ability to execute, especially in the challenging U.S. market.
"While ziltivekimab did not achieve the MACE benefit we had hoped for, this does not change our strategic commitment to cardiovascular disease," chief scientific officer Martin Holst Lange said.

Copenhagen-listed shares were last seen down 7.4% while its American depositary receipts were 8.6% lower in premarket trading, on track for their worst day since February when the company released disappointing results from a head-to-head trial of its next-generation weight-loss drug CagriSema versus Eli Lilly's rival medicine. If losses hold, shares will turn negative for the year.
Jefferies and Citi analysts both said the share move seemed disproportionate given ziltivekimab's small contribution to Novo's overall portfolio.

However, "the result is strategically negative as it removes one of Novo's more credible non-obesity growth opportunities and again reinforces the company's reliance on commercial execution in obesity and sourcing external innovation for driving growth," Jefferies said.

Novo Nordisk Stock Rises After Wegovy Pill Captured 89% of U.S. Prescriptions
sum: Novo Nordisk (NYSE:NVO) shares rose about 2% on Wednesday after new prescription data indicated its oral weight-loss drug Wegovy continued to lead the U.S. market over Eli Lilly's Foundayo.

The report, based on IQVIA data for the week ended July 3, showed the Wegovy pill generated about 153,050 U.S. prescriptions, compared with roughly 19,550 for Foundayo. That gave Novo Nordisk an estimated 89% share of prescriptions for the two once-daily oral obesity medicines, while Eli Lilly accounted for about 11%.

Novo Nordisk introduced the oral version of Wegovy earlier this year, while Eli Lilly launched Foundayo in April. Even after accounting for Novo's earlier market entry, JPMorgan said Wegovy has maintained a sizable lead. During Week 13 of its U.S. rollout, the Wegovy pill recorded about 105,000 prescriptions, more than five times Foundayo's tally at a comparable stage.

The prescription trends have also prompted analysts to revise forecasts. Deutsche Bank lowered its 2026 sales estimate for Foundayo to $1.3 billion from about $3 billion, while FactSet consensus projections for the Wegovy pill have more than doubled to about $2.2 billion for 2026.
